patients.label: 69-year-old woman with Addison’s disease and adrenal crisis after denosumab

fields.index_subject_description: 69-year-old woman with a 35-year history of primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison’s disease) due to adrenalitis, who developed adrenal crisis after subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg for osteoporosis
fields.care_setting: Endocrinology clinic (long-term follow-up); Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Department (admission); Emergency Department (presentation with adrenal crisis)
fields.chief_complaint: Marked weakness and near-syncope at Emergency Department presentation; earlier admission to Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation for fatigue, myalgia and dorsalgia

evidence.quote: A 69-year-old female patient with a 35-year history of primary adrenal insufficiency due to adrenalitis was followed in the endocrinology clinic.
The patient was admitted to the Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Department complaining of fatigue, myalgia, and dorsalgia.
On the following day, she presented to the Emergency Department with marked weakness and near-syncope.

facts.clinical_statement: Single-patient case: adrenal crisis after denosumab in a woman with primary adrenal insufficiency
facts.notes: Multi-setting case; each setting is separately documented. Setting of denosumab administration and of the post-ED hydrocortisone treatment is not stated.

fields.name: Adrenal crisis
fields.diagnostic_basis: Low 8 a.m. cortisol (12 mcg/dL) with elevated ACTH on background of known primary adrenal insufficiency

evidence.quote: An 8 a.m. serum cortisol measured before steroid administration was 12 mcg/dL, inappropriately low for the severity of illness, with elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), confirming adrenal crisis on the background of known primary adrenal insufficiency.
Laboratory evaluation revealed hyponatremia, elevated creatinine, and low morning cortisol with elevated adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH), confirming adrenal crisis.
she developed profound fatigue, vomiting, dizziness, and hypotension

facts.clinical_statement: Adrenal crisis after denosumab administration, confirmed by low cortisol with elevated ACTH
facts.notes: Resolved per "full clinical recovery" (abstract). Association with denosumab is temporal/possible (see ambiguities).

evidence.quote: Laboratory evaluation revealed hyponatremia
Hyponatremia was consistent with cortisol deficiency-mediated antidiuretic hormone excess.

facts.notes: Authors attribute it to cortisol-deficiency-mediated antidiuretic hormone excess; mechanism is author interpretation. Serum sodium 128 mmol/L is recorded in observations.

evidence.quote: Chest X-ray, ECG, and troponin I level showed no evidence of acute infection or cardiac event.
Infectious, cardiac, gastrointestinal, and pharmacokinetic triggers - including medications known to accelerate glucocorticoid metabolism - were excluded.

Several potential alternative etiologies were systematically excluded in this case. Infectious triggers were unlikely, given the absence of fever, normal leukocyte count, negative blood and urine cultures, and unremarkable chest radiography.

facts.clinical_statement: Acute infection not found; infectious trigger excluded/unlikely
facts.notes: Abstract and discussion say alternative etiologies were excluded; the discussion words infection specifically as "unlikely". Kept as absent/refuted because the authors class it among the excluded triggers.

summary.text: A 69-year-old woman with a 35-year history of primary adrenal insufficiency due to adrenalitis, on stable oral prednisolone 5 mg/day with no adrenal crisis for 25 years, had chronic kidney disease (creatinine 1.51 mg/dL, GFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m² in Table 1) and was admitted to Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation with fatigue, myalgia and dorsalgia. Examination was unremarkable except thoracic kyphosis.

DEXA showed postmenopausal osteoporosis (T-scores lumbar spine -3.5, left femur neck -2.4, left femur total -1.6). Because of renal impairment, subcutaneous denosumab 60 mg was chosen instead of bisphosphonates, with no stress-dose prednisolone increase. She also received paracetamol, cholecalciferol, calcium carbonate and exercise therapy.

About 24 hours after the injection she developed progressive fatigue, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, dizziness and skin darkening; the next day she presented to the Emergency Department with marked weakness and near-syncope, hypotension (80/50 mmHg), dehydration, hyponatremia (128 mmol/L), creatinine 1.73 mg/dL, 8 a.m. cortisol 12 mcg/dL (called inappropriately low) with elevated ACTH, confirming adrenal crisis. Cultures were negative, chest X-ray and ECG showed no evidence of acute infection or cardiac event, and alternative triggers were excluded. The authors describe a temporal, possibly causal association (Naranjo score 7, probable).

She received intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg bolus then 50 mg every six hours with isotonic saline and dextrose; oral prednisolone was held. Blood pressure and symptoms improved within 24 hours and sodium and potassium normalized over 72 hours; hydrocortisone was stopped and prednisolone restarted. Discharge values are in Table 1. At six months she was well on prednisolone 5 mg daily.
Table 1 reports vital signs and laboratory values before denosumab administration, after administration and at discharge, with printed reference ranges.
